name: Standard Scramble
approach: Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT trailhead) at Snoqualmie Pass West, reached via I-90 Exit 52 — this is the road-access endpoint; from the trailhead the hike itself begins on the newer rerouted Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Follow the PCT for roughly 2–2.5 miles of well-graded, well-maintained trail through old-growth forest with blueberry and salmonberry understory, gaining a gentle ~2,000 ft over the first 4.5 miles combined. At the signed junction, leave the PCT and turn left (west) onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, following it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek in the basin, which is the one reliable natural water source on the approach (treat before drinking) — carry enough water above this point since the final scramble slopes are dry. As the trail levels out near a small tarn/pond below Red Mountain's west slope, watch for a cairn planted in the middle of the path — this marks the scramble takeoff point where you leave the maintained trail. An alternate, rougher approach follows the older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin Trail starting about 20 yards up from the parking lot, switchbacking directly up into the basin and rejoining near the same trail split (bear right toward Red Pass); it's shorter but harder to follow and not recommended in poor visibility. From the cairn, pick up a boot path climbing the west slope; the track is intermittent and easy to lose on scree, so stay close to the ridge crest on climber's right (south) if you're unsure of the line. The final roughly 900 ft over the last half mile is the crux of the approach: a 30–40° slope of fractured red (iron-stained) rock, loose scree, heather, and scattered alpine trees, alternating Class 2 and low Class 3 scrambling with no real exposure — hands are needed intermittently but it's non-technical. This upper slope holds snow into early summer and can present avalanche/glissade hazard in spring conditions; by mid-to-late summer it's typically dry but still loose and slick when wet.

approach_variants.name: PCT and Commonwealth Creek trail to the cairn by the tarn, then the west-slope boot path
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass West, I-90 exit 52. Follow the rerouted PCT north roughly 2 to 2.5 miles of well-graded trail through old growth. At the signed junction, turn left (west) onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, and follow it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek, the one reliable water on the approach — fill up there, because the scramble slopes above are dry.

An older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin trail leaves about 20 yards up from the parking lot and switchbacks directly into the basin, rejoining near the same split. It is shorter, harder to follow, and not recommended in poor visibility.

About 12.9 km round trip and 2,900 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Snow lingers in Commonwealth Basin and on the upper slope into early-to-mid July, and the fractured rock is genuinely unsafe wet, so late July to September is the sweet spot
hazards: Rockfall on loose, heavily fractured red rock, with documented close calls near the summit
Slick, dangerous rock when wet — an easy class 2 slope becomes unsafe in rain
Route-finding above the basin tarn where maintained trail becomes a cairned boot path
Lingering snow and postholing into early summer
Cliffed-out class 3-4 ground if a party tries to shortcut east toward the Kendall Katwalk
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The takeoff is marked by a cairn planted in the middle of the path, and that is the arrival test. As the trail levels out near a small tarn below Red Mountain's west slope, a cairn sits in the middle of the tread. That is where the scramble leaves the maintained trail. A cairn off to one side is not it; this one is in the way, deliberately.

From the cairn, what the ground should do: a boot path climbs the west slope. It is intermittent and easy to lose on scree. The rule when you lose it is to stay close to the ridge crest on climbers' right — the south side. That single rule replaces route-finding for the whole upper slope, and it also keeps you off the loose gut of the scree where you would be kicking rock onto people.

What the last 900 ft should feel like: a 30 to 40 degree slope of fractured, iron-stained red rock, loose scree, heather and scattered alpine trees, alternating class 2 and low class 3, with no real exposure. Hands needed intermittently. If you are on genuinely exposed ground with real fall consequence, you have drifted off the line.

And the most important negative, which is about the descent but belongs here: do not traverse east or south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Katwalk as a shortcut. That terrain becomes class 3 and 4 and cliffs out without a rope.

Honest note on the rock: helmets are for the whole party, not just a leader. Red Mountain's rock is notoriously fractured and there are documented close calls with softball- and grapefruit-sized rock near the summit.

days.note: Standard day trip from the PCT North Trailhead: hike the PCT to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction, follow it up into Commonwealth Basin to the small pond below Red Mountain's west face, then take the cairned climber's boot path up open slopes, ledges, and scree/heather gullies to the summit. Descend the same west-slope/southwest-ridge line back to the pond and out.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble

schedule.label: Leave PCT North Trailhead
schedule.detail: Elevation ~3,000 ft; parking fills on weekends.

schedule.label: Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033) junction
schedule.detail: 2 miles up the PCT, then turn off onto #1033 toward Red Pass/Red Mountain.

schedule.label: Reach the pond below the west face
schedule.detail: ~4.5 mi and ~4,600 ft mark; look for the cairn/boot path leaving the trail.

schedule.label: Ascend boot path to summit
schedule.detail: Hands-on scrambling across ledges, scree gullies, and heather; some parties report noon summits on an 8 AM start.

schedule.label: Summit (5,890 ft)
schedule.detail: Rock-bench seating at the top; typical stay 15–30 min.

schedule.label: Descend same route to trailhead
schedule.detail: Descent runs faster than the ascent, roughly 2.5 hours back to the car.

days.objective: Summit via the west-slope boot path

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day: ~8 miles round trip, 2,900 ft gain, typically 5.5–7 hours car-to-car (this account's ascent 3.8 hr / descent 2.4 hr).
